abstract: Although ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes are critical regulators of cellular function and fate, their roles in tumorigenesis remain incompletely defined. Here, we provide genetic and molecular evidence that the Ubiquitin-Conjugating Enzyme E2 D3 (UBE2D3) is specifically overexpressed in cancerous pancreatic ductal cells, including early-stage pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia and advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). This overexpression is independent of oncogenic KRAS status and is driven by the inflammatory tumor microenvironment, particularly interferon-γ (IFN-γ). Mechanistically, UBE2D3 binds the ubiquitin ligase Kelch Like Family Member 13 (KLHL13) to mediate K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine 245 of transporter 2 (TAP2), resulting in steric hindrance that blocks the transporter. Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of UBE2D3 enhances antigen presentation in cancer cells and restores CD8 + T-cell-mediated tumor surveillance in pancreatic cancer models in male mice. Furthermore, combining an UBE2D3 small-molecule inhibitor with KRAS G12D -specific TCR-T-cell therapy yields synergistic antitumor effects. Our findings reveal a negative feedback mechanism in which cancer cells, “camouflaging” themselves, evade IFN-γ-induced antigen presentation via UBE2D3 upregulation, highlighting a potential therapeutic target for enhancing antitumor immunity.

Following the determination of cell lysate protein concentrations, lysates containing 1–3 mg of total protein were absorbed into EP tubes at 200–400 μL with a concentration of 10 mg/mL. Simultaneously, 1–4 μg of specific antibody and 150–300 μL of incubation solution were added, and the antibody concentration was optimized via titration. For the molecular docking of UBE2D3 and QX-6, the crystal structure of the UBE2D3 protein (PDB ID: 1×23) was downloaded from RCSB. The HDOCK server was used to dock the UBE2D3 protein with the small molecule QX-6. The conformation with the highest docking score was chosen for subsequent analysis. The QX-6 kinetic simulation was conducted via GROMACS. The receptor and ligand force fields were generated via the ATB server, employing the GROMOS 54A7 force field type. The process involved 50,000 steps of energy minimization to remove unfavorable contacts in the initial structure, followed by 100 ps of NVT (constant particle number, volume, and temperature) equilibration, 100 ps of NPT (constant particle number, pressure, and temperature) equilibration, and finally, 100 ns of simulation runs. The RMSD value was calculated for the dynamics. The last 10 ns (90–100 ns) of the simulation tracks were selected to be saved at 100 ps intervals, and the binding free energy was calculated via the gmx_MMPBSA 10 scripting tool.

Introduction
Tumor-promoting inflammation, a well-established hallmark of cancer, is evident at the earliest stages of neoplastic progression and fosters the development of incipient neoplasias into full-blown cancers
1
. Paradoxically, growing evidence suggests that in various tumor types, tumor-antagonistic immune cells, such as NK cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), can enhance cancer potential by releasing pluripotent bioactive molecules into the tumor microenvironment (TME), exerting selective pressure on cancer cells to evade immune destruction
2
,
3
.
In canonical immunity, proinflammatory factors such as IFN-γ enhance MHC class I antigen processing and presentation and amplify immune responses
4
; however, in chronic tumor-associated inflammation, sustained low-dose IFN-γ exposure can promote tumorigenesis through mechanisms including IFN-γ desensitization, MHC class I downregulation, and T-cell exhaustion
5
,
6
. The molecular basis for impaired antigen presentation under inflammatory conditions remains unclear.
Ubiquitination plays a central role in antigen degradation, antigen processing, and the stability and function of antigen-presenting molecules, thereby ensuring effective antigen presentation and immune surveillance
7
–
9
. Dysregulation of ubiquitinating enzymes such as UBE2T, UBE2N, RNF43, and WWP2 has been linked to immune evasion and cancer immune evasion through degradation of MHC-I, PD-1, and STAT3
10
–
18
. Ubiquitin modifications, akin to codes, can take various conformations, such as monoubiquitylation, multimonoubiquitylation, and polyubiquitylation chains (e.g., K48 or K63), resulting in diverse cellular outcomes beyond substrate degradation
7
,
8
,
19
. In which E2 enzymes, guided by E3 ligases (especially those with RING or U-box domains), determine substrate ubiquitin linkage specificity
20
,
21
. However, the role of E2s in inflammation-driven immune evasion, particularly in antigen presentation, remains poorly understood. Collectively, these observations prompted us to identify E2 enzymes involved in dysregulated antigen presentation, aiming to expand our understanding of protumor inflammation-mediated immune evasion.
In this work, we identify the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2D3 as a key player in the tumor-promoting, inflammation-mediated immune escape of pancreatic cancer. Mechanically, IFN-γ microenvironment induces cancer cell UBE2D3 overexpression, and this enzyme contributes to the downregulation of the antigen presentation pathway via ubiquitination-blocking peptide transporter. Targeted inhibition of UBE2D3 enzyme activity enhances the anti-tumor immune response, providing a potential therapeutic strategy.
Results
Elevated UBE2D3 expression is correlated with tumorigenesis and progression in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
Tumor development is generally considered a multistep process in which the accumulation of genetic variants, such as driver mutations and passenger mutations, plays a crucial role
22
. To identify molecular aberrations in the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2) family, we examined their genetic profiles across 33 tumor types in the TCGA-PanCancer Atlas. As shown in Supplementary Fig.
1a
, E2 enzymes exhibit few genome-level mutations, such as frameshift, splicing, amplification, depletion, and structural variations, but they present a considerable number of alterations at the mRNA level. The transcriptome profile of PanCancer (Supplementary Fig.
1b
) revealed that the mRNA levels of E2 enzyme signatures were elevated in a variety of tumor tissues compared with those in paired normal tissues, especially in cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD), and thymoma (THYM) tissues. Although E2 signatures were differentially expressed in all four cancer types, the unusually high mortality rate of PAAD, with a five-year survival rate of less than 10% and a rising global incidence, prompted us to further analyze the expression features of E2 signatures within the TCGA-PAAD dataset (Supplementary Fig.
2a
). A total of 26 differentially expressed E2s out of 39 E2s were identified, including
ATG3
,
UBE2A
,
UBE2C
, and
UBE2D1-3
. Among these,
UBE2T
, previously reported as a highly expressed E2 in pancreatic cancer, promotes the degradation of p53 in cancer cells
15
; however, despite the known role of
UBE2F
in promoting pancreatic tumor development
23
, we did not observe significant differences in
UBE2F
levels.
To identify key E2 members with the potential to influence patient outcomes, we analyzed their transcriptome expression levels and clinical annotations in the TCGA-PAAD dataset. Eight E2 members—
UBE2C
,
UBE2D3
,
UBE2H
,
UBE2I
,
UBE2K
,
UBE2L3
,
UBE2L6
, and
UBE2T
—were identified as prognostic risk factors. Notably, compared with other risk E2 members,
UBE2D3
has the highest transcriptomic expression level in tumor tissues and plays a crucial role in the degradation of the tumor suppressor p53, leading to cancer cell proliferation and survival
24
–
26
. To investigate the potential causal relationship between
UBE2D3
expression levels and patient prognosis, we examined UBE2D3 protein levels in pancreatic samples of various pathological types, including pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm (PNEN), solid pseudopapillary tumor of the pancreas (SPTP), pancreatic serous cystic neoplasm (PSCN), acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas (ASCP), pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) samples. Interestingly, the immunohistochemical data revealed that UBE2D3 was predominantly highly expressed in PanIN and PDAC samples, whereas its expression was minimal in normal pancreatic tissues and adjacent noncancer tissues (Fig.
1a, b
). It is commonly believed that PDAC, which accounts for more than 90% of all pancreatic cancers, originates from acinar-ductal metaplasia and PanIN progression and is accompanied by multiple genetic alterations
27
. To explore whether
UBE2D3
could serve as an independent prognostic factor, we compared overall survival across different expression stratifications in two public datasets (TCGA and GEO). Our analysis revealed a consistent association between
UBE2D3
levels and patient risk, with high expression correlating with worse prognosis (50% high, HR = 1.5; 60% high, HR = 1.6; 80% high, HR = 1.9), which was distinct from other E2D subtypes in the TCGA-PAAD dataset (Supplementary Fig.
2b
). This prognostic signature was further validated in an independent PDAC dataset from
GSE57495
(Supplementary Fig.
2c
). Encouraged by these findings, we continued to explore UBE2D3 protein levels and their relationship with patient survival. Survival data were available for 48 of the 53 patients. As shown in Supplementary Fig.
2d
, a high UBE2D3 level was associated with a trend toward worse prognosis compared to a low UBE2D3 level (
P
= 0.043). These results indicate that UBE2D3 overexpression is an early molecular event in PDAC tumorigenesis and remains elevated across different tumor stages.

UBE2D3 overexpression is primarily observed within intratumoral cancer cells
To investigate the role of UBE2D3 in PDAC development, we first identified which subcellular populations within PDAC tumors presented abnormally increased UBE2D3 expression. Immunohistochemistry data from patients with PanIN and PDAC suggested that UBE2D3 is expressed primarily in cancerous ductal epithelial cells (Fig.
1a
). To gain a more detailed understanding of UBE2D3 expression in tumors, we generated KPC cells stably expressing GFP and orthotopically implanted them into C57BL/6 mice. This allowed us to assess Ube2d3 levels in both tumor and nontumor cells in vivo by flow cytometric (Fig.
1c, d

3
). Here, we identified two distinct subcellular populations with significantly higher Ube2d3 MFI levels: intratumoral cancer cells and tumor-infiltrating B lymphocytes (Fig.

In contrast to intratumoral cancer cells, tumor-infiltrating B lymphocytes exhibited obvious heterogeneity in Ube2d3 expression, indicating that the high MFI levels detected are attributable to a minority of highly expressing B-cell subpopulations (Fig.
1d

Ube2d3

4

Ube2d3
WT/KO

KO

WT

In fact, cancer cells were more abundant in the population, constituting approximately >10% of live singlets, compared to tumor-infiltrating B lymphocytes, which make up around 0.8% of live singlets. Thus, it is reasonable to infer that the increased UBE2D3 levels are derived primarily from cancer cells within the tumor. It is well known that the Jak/STAT pathway is activated by proinflammatory factors such as IFN and IL-6, as well as growth factors, thereby inducing the expression of downstream genes
32

12

The results showed that treating murine PDAC cell lines with the STAT3 inhibitor (STAT3i) Stattic did not alter the baseline Ube2d3 level but effectively blocked TIF-induced Ube2d3 expression (Supplementary Fig.
5b
). Interestingly, in two human PDAC cells (PANC-1 and MIA PaCa-2), we observed that IFN-γ primarily activated STAT3 rather than STAT1, and IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression was obviously dose-dependent (Fig.
2d
, left and middle panels). In contrast, BxPC-3 cells were reported to exhibit stronger activation of STAT1 over STAT3 in response to IFN-γ

, along with a slight dose-dependent upregulation of IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression (Fig.
2d
, right panel). In line with this, IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression was also time-dependent. In PANC-1 cells, UBE2D3 and phosphorylated STAT3 (p-STAT3) levels were elevated at 6 h post-IFN-γ treatment, returning to baseline levels by 48 h post-treatment (Fig.
2e
), and the STAT3 inhibitor significantly inhibited IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression (Fig.
2f
).
Furthermore, to explore whether UBE2D3 levels are also dependent on endogenous factors such as the status of proto-oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes

7a, b

7b

7b

35

36

This can be concluded consistently through a co-expression analysis in PDAC patient tumors, that UBE2D3 levels were significantly associated with p-STAT3 levels rather than p-STAT1 levels (Fig.

To investigate whether STAT1/3 directly activates UBE2D3 expression as a transcription factor, we first used JASPAR to predict potential STAT1/3 binding sites in the UBE2D3 promoter. 8a

Based on these predictions, we conducted a series of UBE2D3 promoter reporter assays, and found that in STAT3-dependent cell lines (e.g., PANC-1 and MIA PaCa-2 cells), IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression relies on the activation of the STAT3 activation rather than STAT1; in contrast, in STAT1-dependent cell lines such as BxPC-3 cells, IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression relies on STAT1 activation (Fig.

To further investigate this phenomenon, we coimmunoprecipitated whole cell lysates with an anti-endogenous UBE2D3 antibody for two human PDAC cell lines and found that UBE2D3 interacts with TAP2 and KLHL13 (Supplementary Fig.
15a
). Similarly, coimmunoprecipitation with an anti-endogenous KLHL3 antibody revealed that KLHL13 interacts with TAP2 and UBE2D3, indicating that the UBE2D3 E2 enzyme may bind the KLHL13 E3 enzyme to ubiquitinate TAP2 (Supplementary Fig.
15b
). The membrane-associated protein encoded by the TAP2 gene belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily
40
, which forms a heterodimer with ABCB2 (TAP1) to transport peptides from the cytoplasm to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Molecular docking of TAP2 with KLHL13 indicated that the cytoplasmic region of TAP2 binds to the BTB domain of KLHL13, with GLN 130 of TAP2 hydrogen bonding to VAL 309 and THR 312 of KLHL13 (Supplementary Fig.
15c, d
). Additionally, molecular docking of TAP2 with UBE2D3 indicated that lysine 245 of TAP2 binds to the UBE2D3 C85 catalytic active pocket, with multiple hydrogen bonds formed between specific residues of TAP2 and UBE2D3 (Supplementary Fig.
15e
).
Thus, we propose that the Cullin-KLHL13 E3 complex connects UBE2D3 and TAP2, guiding the ubiquitination of TAP2 by UBE2D3. Consistently, immunofluorescence staining of TAP2, UBE2D3, and KLHL13 in PDAC patient tumors revealed colocalization in the ER (Supplementary Fig.

In line with this, a cell-free E2 selectivity assay revealed that all UBE2D subtypes could ubiquitinate TAP2 substrates, with UBE2D3 being the most effective, followed by UBE2D1 and UBE2D2, which have 79% and 87% homology with UBE2D3, respectively, whereas UBE2D4 has the lowest homology at 70% (Supplementary Fig.
15g
). These findings indicate that the UBE2D3-KLHL13 complex ubiquitinates the peptide transporter TAP2, providing insights into the mechanism of UBE2D3-mediated blockage of antigen presentation in cancer cells.
K63-linked polyubiquitin on lysine 245 of TAP2 forms a steric hindrance that blocks antigen peptide transport
LC/MS data indicated that the total TAP2 protein level in Ube2d3 KO KPC cells remained unchanged, whereas the level of ubiquitinated TAP2 was significantly decreased. Western blot assays further confirmed that Ube2d3 KO and Klhl13 KO did not significantly affect TAP2 protein levels in KPC cells (Fig.
5d
). Considering that ubiquitin polymeric chain modifications can affect protein stability, activation, subcellular localization, and signal transduction
19
, we further examined the ubiquitin chain modification of TAP2 by UBE2D3. Our results demonstrated that in PANC-1 cells, UBE2D3 exhibits the ability to catalyze both K48- and K63-linked polyubiquitination
41
, and can mediate these modifications on TAP2 substrates, with a preference for K63-linked polyubiquitin chains. Specifically, we found that UBE2D3 predominantly modifies TAP2 at K245 (equivalent to K244 in mouse TAP2) with K63-linked polyubiquitin, rather than K48-linked polyubiquitin, which typically signals the protein for proteasomal degradation (Fig.
5e
). Previous studies have shown that K63-linked polyubiquitination is crucial for MAVS aggregation, activating innate immune pathways
42
. However, the effect of K63-linked polyubiquitin at the K245 site of TAP2 remains unclear.
To investigate this, we constructed three TAP2 molecular crystal structures, namely, the wildtype, K245-monomeric ubiquitin modification, and K245-K63 polyubiquitin modification, and performed molecular docking simulations with TAP1 (Fig.
5f
). The results showed that TAP2 with K63-poly ubiquitin modification forms a stronger bond with TAP1, indicating either a more difficult opening of the TAP1/TAP2 complex transport pocket or greater steric hindrance restricting peptide transport. Consistently, we observed that compared with TAP2-MUT, TAP2-WT ectopic expression can accumulate more K63-ubiquitination modifications under the action of UBE2D3 (Fig.
5g
). In addition, pMHC-I (H-2K
b
-SIINFEK) levels on the surface of Ube2d3 KO and/or Klhl13 KO KPC
OVA
cells significantly increased under mIFN-γ stimulation (Fig.
5h
). Moreover, overexpressing the murine K244R mutant TAP2 in KPC
OVA
cells resulted in higher pMHC-I levels than did wild-type TAP2, and this trend was reversed by re-expressing Ube2d3 (Fig.
5i
).
To explore the steric blocking of ubiquitination on TAP2, we conducted TAP transport assays on streptolysin-O (SLO) permeabilized KPC cells with Ube2d3 overexpression or knockdown. The results showed that Ube2d3 overexpression inhibited TAP FITC-labeled peptide transport capacity, while Ube2d3 inhibition significantly enhanced mIFN-γ-induced TAP FITC-labeled peptide transport (Fig.
5j
, k). Additionally, to investigate the effect of ubiquitination modification of the K245 site on TAP steric blocking, we ectopically co-expressed WT TAP1/TAP2 and WT TAP1/ K245R mutant TAP2 in T2 cells, which lack endogenous TAP, and assessed their TAP transport capacity following SLO permeabilization. The results demonstrated that ubiquitination of TAP2 at K245 by UBE2D3 is crucial for TAP peptide transport capacity (Fig.
5l
).
Our findings demonstrate that UBE2D3, guided by KLHL13, localizes to the ER and modifies the K245 (mouse, K244) site of TAP2 via K63-linked polyubiquitination. This modification results in a functional block of the TAP1/TAP2 complex, thereby inhibiting peptide transfer and impacting antigen presentation.

Discussion
We propose a mechanism for impaired antigen presentation in PDAC (Supplementary Fig.
19
), where chronic inflammatory exposure, specifically IFN-γ, triggers UBE2D3-mediated ubiquitin signaling in cancer cells, leading to the ubiquitination of TAP1/2 transporters and blocking IFN-γ activation of the antigen-presenting pathway. Genetic or pharmacological interference with UBE2D3 enzyme activity improves antigen-presenting potential of cancer cells, thereby increasing their susceptibility to cytotoxic CD8
+
T-cell immune attacks. These data suggest that UBE2D3 overexpression in cancer cells represents a “stress sensor/effector” for tumor-promoting inflammation. In this study, one concern is whether this finding is specific to PDAC. Research is currently underway to investigate whether IFN-γ regulates UBE2D3 expression in other tumor types, where we also observed unusually high expression in glioblastoma (GBM) tumor tissues compared with normal tissues in the TCGA dataset (Supplementary Fig.
20
). A recent study has shown that in GBM, UBE2D3 plays a role in creating a proinflammatory environment by recruiting myeloid cells
50
.
While tumor-promoting inflammation has been established as a cornerstone of cancer immune escape
1
,
51
, the underlying mechanisms of action of inflammatory factors are incompletely understood. One major reason is that these cytokines are often pluripotent. For example, IFN-γ serves as an immune mediator with both protumor and antitumor functions
6
. This duality is thought to be related to the IFN-γ concentration in the TME. Persistent low-dose exposure to IFN-γ enables cancer cells to acquire multiple hallmark characteristics, whereas transient high-dose exposure inhibits cancer cell proliferation and activates antitumor immunity. This low-dose IFN-γ exposure is attributed to the low immunogenicity of endogenous antigens in cancer cells, immature differentiation of immune cells such as dendritic cells (DCs), and poor activation of tumor-specific CD4
+
or CD8
+
T cells
52
–
54
. The immunosuppressive effect of low-dose IFN-γ is being investigated. Numerous studies have indicated that persistent IFN-γ signaling in cancer cells drives p-STAT1 activation and mediates the synthesis of immunosuppressive molecules such as PD-L1, IDO, and TNFRSF14
55
,
56
while also suppressing stem-like features and inducing apoptosis in cytotoxic T cells
5
. Our findings suggest that IFN-γ in PDAC not only directly promotes the activation of the antigen-presenting pathway in pancreatic cancer but also triggers a set of negative feedback mechanisms within the cell, termed intracellular immune checkpoints
57
. In this context, IFN-γ activates p-STAT3 to promote the transcription of UBE2D3, resulting in increased ubiquitination of the ER cytoplasmic domain K245 in the peptide transport complex subunit TAP2. The polyubiquitination modification at this specific site does not lead to TAP2 degradation but instead creates steric hindrance, preventing the transport of peptides into the ER and the subsequent assembly of MHC-I. This is significantly different from other observations of immune escape via ubiquitination-mediated MHC-I degradation
18
,
58
,
59
. Unsurprisingly, ubiquitination appears to block peptide transport more quickly and economically than does ubiquitination, which degrades MHC-I pathway components. In fact, we did not observe a significant change in total MHC-I (H-2K
b
) or TAP2 levels after UBE2D3 KO. The functional transformation, rather than the degradation of target proteins induced by ubiquitination, highlighted in our study, can provide implications for related research. A previous study indicated that IFN-γ treatment of PDAC cells in vitro can upregulate MHC-I and TAP levels, facilitating CD8
+
T-cell responses
60
. This process aligns with our current understanding of the canonical functions of IFN-γ
4
. Our study further revealed the mechanism by which UBE2D3 negatively regulates this inflammatory response. Overall, our study highlights the functional transformation rather than degradation of ubiquitinated TAP2, which has significant implications for the study of posttranslational modifications related to antigen presentation pathways.
UBE2D3, an E2 enzyme with a UBC core domain, catalyzes the formation of free or anchored polyubiquitin chains independently of E3 ligases
7
,
13
,
21
. In our study, we identified the ubiquitin modification of TAP2 by UBE2D3 E2 conjugating enzyme guided by Cullin-RING E3 ligase (KLHL13). UBE2D3 and Cullin-KLHL3/12 E2-E3 pairs have been reported to play regulatory roles in protein transport and ion cotransport
61
,
62
. Similarly, our study identified a regulatory mechanism of UBE2D3 and Cullin-KLHL13 E2-E3 pair on peptide transport in TAP. Furthermore, several studies have reported that UBE2D3 collaborates with other E3 ligases, such as RNF138 and UHRF1
63
,
64
. LC/MS did not detect any significant changes in the ubiquitination levels of these two single-ring finger E3 enzymes, while members of the HECT-type and multi-subunit RING-finger E3 enzyme families were identified. Interestingly, we observed that UBE2D3 KO significantly upregulated the ubiquitination levels of HSP70/90, proteins involved in peptide transport to the ER. This suggests the presence of potential negative regulatory mechanisms.
Studies on tumor biology suggest that UBE2D3 is critical for regulating metabolic pathways and inflammatory responses in cancer cells
11
,
12
. Notably, in U87 and T98G GBM cell lines, the inhibition of UBE2D3 suppresses cancer cell proliferation and STAT3 phosphorylation
12
. Our study demonstrated that inhibiting UBE2D3 in PDAC does not affect cancer cell colony formation or proliferation, but blocking STAT3 phosphorylation inhibits IFN-γ-induced UBE2D3 expression, indicating that STAT3 activation is required for UBE2D3 overexpression. The difference in survival between these two types of cell lines may be due to variations in biological background; however, a strong association was observed between UBE2D3 and p-STAT3. A UBE2D3‒p-STAT3 feedback loop is suggested, and studies are underway to confirm this.
MHC class I antigen processing and presentation are essential for the adaptive immune response of tumor-specific T cells
65
, and aberrations in peptide transport, such as TAP1/2 frameshift mutation and protein dysfunction, enable tumor cells to develop immune escape capabilities
66
,
67
. Our identification of UBE2D3-mediated TAP2 ubiquitination is a significant addition to understanding defects in the TAP1/2 complex in cancer. More importantly, these findings establish a foundation for the immunotherapy of pancreatic cancer. We propose that UBE2D3 inhibition (UBE2D3i) can be combined with various immune activation agents, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, oncolytic viruses, and ACT therapies. Here, we present an example of UEB2D3 inhibition in KRAS-targeted TCR-T-cell therapy. This consideration is because improvements in pMHC-I may be more suitable for antigen-targeted T-cell therapies. A study reported a 72% response rate for visceral cancer regression in a metastatic pancreatic cancer patient treated with engineered HLA-C*08:02-restricted KRAS
G12D
TCR T cells
45
. In addition, the dense fibrotic stroma of the PDAC TME creates a barrier that impedes immune cell infiltration; CAR-T cells, with high antigenic target affinity, often face peripheral blockage in solid tumors, whereas TCR-T cells, with lower TCR-pMHC-I affinity, can penetrate deeper, bypassing surface antigens pulled at the tumor periphery
68
,
69
.
We showed that UBE2D3 mediates K63-linked polyubiquitination on TAP2, thereby sterically blocking peptide transport, inhibiting antigen assembly and presentation. However, due to current testing technology, accurately quantifying the proportion of K63 ubiquitinated TAP2 within the total TAP2 pool and fully elucidating the precise mechanism by which ubiquitination sterically blocks the TAP complex remains challenging.
Although a comprehensive portfolio of PDAC models, including in vivo PDX models, was investigated, it remains unclear whether PDACs with high or low UBE2D3 expression engage the UBE2D3-TAP2 pathway to evade the immune system. Further investigation is needed to explore the differences in TAP steric blocking between these groups.

TAP2 molecular docking
For the molecular docking of TAP2, KLHL13, and UBE2D3, the crystal structures of the TAP2 protein (PDB ID: 5U1D, B chain) and UBE2D3 protein (PDB ID: 1 × 23) were obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank. The predicted crystal structure of the KLHL13 protein (AF-
Q9P2N7
-F1) was downloaded from the AlphaFold protein structure database. To optimize the conformation for molecular docking, the KLHL13 protein underwent a 50 ns kinetic simulation via Gromacs 2021.
Next, we utilized the HDOCK server for molecular docking. The BTB domain of the KLHL13 protein and the cytoplasmic region of the TAP2 protein were docked. The best fit, or Top1 conformation, was chosen on the basis of the docking area criteria. Similarly, the K245 site of the TAP2 protein and the C85 site in the active pocket of the UBE2D3 protein were docked. After the fits were evaluated, the Top3 conformation was selected for further analysis according to the docking area requirements.
For the molecular docking of TAP1 with ubiquitin-modified TAP2, the crystal structures of the TAP1 protein (PDB ID: 5U1D, A chain) and ubiquitin protein (PDB ID: 1D3Z) were downloaded from RCSB. We constructed a structure of TAP2 with ubiquitin (Ub) modification, where the amino acid Ub G76 is covalently linked to the K245 amino acid of TAP2, and a structure of TAP2 with K63-polyubiquitin (Ub) modification, where another amino acid, Ub G76, is covalently linked to the K63 amino acid of the Ub modified on TAP2. The HDOCK server was used to dock TAP1 with TAP2, TAP2 (K245) monoubiquitin, and TAP2 (K245) K63-linked polyubiquitin.
QX-6 molecular docking and dynamics simulation
For the molecular docking of UBE2D3 and QX-6, the crystal structure of the UBE2D3 protein (PDB ID: 1×23) was downloaded from RCSB. The HDOCK server was used to dock the UBE2D3 protein with the small molecule QX-6. The conformation with the highest docking score was chosen for subsequent analysis. The QX-6 kinetic simulation was conducted via GROMACS. The receptor and ligand force fields were generated via the ATB server, employing the GROMOS 54A7 force field type. The process involved 50,000 steps of energy minimization to remove unfavorable contacts in the initial structure, followed by 100 ps of NVT (constant particle number, volume, and temperature) equilibration, 100 ps of NPT (constant particle number, pressure, and temperature) equilibration, and finally, 100 ns of simulation runs. The RMSD value was calculated for the dynamics. The last 10 ns (90–100 ns) of the simulation tracks were selected to be saved at 100 ps intervals, and the binding free energy was calculated via the gmx_MMPBSA 10 scripting tool.
